headline: Subadditivity: compare the whole with a valid breakdown
lede: A detailed risk list can change a probability judgement without adding evidence. Before comparing the total with its parts, check that you are asking the same question and that every case belongs to exactly one part.

sections.heading: What changes when a category is unpacked
paragraphs: The subadditivity effect concerns subjective probability judgements. A person may give one estimate for a broad event and a larger combined estimate when that event is described as several possibilities. The event has not changed. Its description has changed, and different possibilities may now come to mind. Support theory provides an account of this pattern, but the evidence does not establish that every detailed description raises a probability estimate.

The distinction matters because a breakdown can also reveal genuinely new information. Learning that a supplier has a production problem is different from hearing a longer list of possible causes of delay. In the first case, there may be evidence for revising the estimate. In the second, a changed estimate needs an explanation. Neither the short description nor the long one is automatically correct.

sections.heading: A worked example with an explicit partition
paragraphs: This is an illustrative calculation, not a report of a study or a real project. Define the event as an order arriving after its agreed date. First record a 20% estimate for that event. Then use three categories: a late order whose first recorded cause is production, one whose first recorded cause is transport, and one whose first recorded cause is anything else. Agree in advance how simultaneous causes will be assigned.

Suppose the separate estimates are 12%, 10% and 8%. They sum to 30%, which differs from the original 20%. Because the categories cover the same late-order event without overlap, the estimates are inconsistent. The comparison exposes that inconsistency. It does not tell us whether 20% or 30% is closer to the actual frequency. That requires evidence about orders, causes and the reliability of the estimates.

sections.heading: Why an ordinary risk list is not enough
paragraphs: A production problem and a transport problem can occur on the same order. Adding their probabilities would then count some orders twice. For overlapping events, the probability of either event equals the sum of their probabilities minus the probability of both. A list that omits other causes has a different problem: its categories do not cover all cases. Either issue can explain a mismatch without demonstrating subadditivity.

Do not confuse mutually exclusive events with independent events. Mutually exclusive categories cannot both contain the same case; independent events are a different mathematical relationship. For this comparison, define a partition that covers every relevant case exactly once. If that is impractical, keep the overlapping risks as a risk register and use a suitable model for their combined probability rather than treating the list as an additive forecast.

sections.heading: Review the estimates without forcing a preferred answer
paragraphs: Keep the packed estimate and the separate estimates visible. Ask what information each was based on, whether the time window stayed the same, and whether the breakdown made a previously overlooked possibility salient. Compare with records from similar orders when those records are available. Revise the whole, the parts, or both when the evidence justifies it. Do not force every component into the original total merely because that number came first.

The reviewed research includes boundary conditions: typical and atypical descriptions can produce different effects, and unpacking need not always increase the combined judgement. A consistency check is useful even when no bias is diagnosed. Record the wording, estimates and reasons for revision so that a later review can inspect what changed. This creates a decision record; it is not evidence that the procedure improves forecasting accuracy in every setting.

sections.heading: How this differs from nearby probability errors
paragraphs: A conjunction error concerns rating a combined event, A and B, as more probable than A alone. Subadditivity concerns a difference between a packed event and the sum of estimates for its parts. Double-counting overlapping risks is an arithmetic or modelling problem that can resemble the latter. Use the definition that fits the actual comparison instead of applying several labels to the same unexplained difference.

A vivid description may affect what comes to mind, but vividness does not establish the real frequency of an event. Likewise, a list of reasons is not a collection of independent pieces of evidence. Separate the probability question from persuasion: a detailed list can help someone understand the possible outcomes without supplying a defensible combined estimate. The evidence review below links the original support-theory work and research on its boundary conditions.

checklist: Keep the event and time window identical in both questions.
Define parts that cover every case exactly once.
Check overlap and missing causes before adding estimates.
Explain differences using evidence rather than enforcing the first number.
Record wording, estimates and reasons so the review can be repeated.
boundaryNote: This editorial guide uses the existing evidence review and its sources. The numerical example is hypothetical. A difference between packed and unpacked estimates does not by itself establish which forecast is accurate or whether a psychological bias caused it.
